title: Who leaves federal agencies first
hook: OPM's raw files showed the Army reporting 9 departures in September 2026. Its September data was incomplete. I check coverage and split out seasonal jobs before ranking anything, then show which agencies lose permanent staff year after year.
metric: Army: 9 separations reported in Sep 2026, 180,217 still employed

trace.problem: Missing data and seasonal jobs skew the ranking
trace.move: Coverage check, permanent staff ranked apart
trace.result: VA and the Army lead permanent-staff quits every year

cardVisual.label: Army separations in OPM's September file

body.problem: Federal turnover numbers mislead in four ways. An agency with incomplete data looks like it kept everyone. People who left in one month show up in later files. Seasonal and temporary jobs end on a schedule and crowd the top of the quit ranking. And in 2025, exit-program departures were mostly coded as resignations, so they read like a wave of quits.
body.approach: I pulled 15 years of OPM separation files and September headcounts through OPM's open API, with a pull that can stop and resume and tracks every file version. A coverage check compares each agency's monthly report with its own previous year and holds failing years out of the ranking. Rates are counted by the month a person left, for all staff and for permanent staff on regular schedules, with exit-program departures split out.
body.hers: Solo project on public data. I designed the question, the checks and the data contract, and built the pull, the SQL tables and the dashboard.
body.result: Seventeen agency-months since Jul 2011 fail the coverage check, including the Army and Air Force in Aug and Sep 2026. Commerce, Interior and Agriculture lead raw quit rates nearly every year, and none of them reaches the top five once seasonal and temporary jobs are left out. Among permanent staff, Veterans Affairs and the Army are in the top five in all 13 complete years from FY2012 to FY2024.
